solution:
**(C)** three

Based on position, meristems are of three types: apical meristem at the tips of root and shoot, intercalary meristem at the top or base of nodes, and lateral meristem along the sides of the central axis. Apical meristem increases length, and lateral meristem increases girth.

**(C)** lateral meristem

Cambium (fascicular, interfascicular and cork cambium) lies along the sides of the central axis of stem and root, so it is a lateral meristem, and it increases the girth of the organ. Apical meristem lies at the tips and increases length. Intercalary meristem lies at the nodes, mainly in monocots, and is short lived.

**(A)** living

Collenchyma is a simple permanent tissue made of living cells with cytoplasm, nucleus and vacuoles; its cell walls are thickened unevenly with cellulose and pectin at the corners. It is the living mechanical tissue of young stems and petioles. Sclerenchyma, by contrast, is made of dead cells at maturity.

**(D)** Xylem

A complex permanent tissue is made of more than one type of cell working as a unit. Xylem consists of tracheids, vessels, xylem parenchyma and xylem fibres, so it is complex (phloem is the other complex tissue). Parenchyma and sclerenchyma are simple permanent tissues made of one cell type, and chlorenchyma is parenchyma that contains chloroplasts, so it is simple too.

**(C)** leaf

Mesophyll is the chloroplast-containing photosynthetic ground tissue between the upper and lower epidermis of a leaf. In a dicot leaf it is differentiated into palisade and spongy parenchyma; in a monocot leaf it is not. Root and stem have cortex and pith as ground tissue, not mesophyll.
